item.title: HNInternal: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do? (427 pts)
item.description:
See on Hacker News


Build something, put it on your resume instead of job. Make it free, try to get users, add testimonials to your resume too.

Makes it a lot easier to explain the gap. “What did you do the last x months?” “This, look”


I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much.

But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree.

I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped.

My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way.

Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it.

Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.


Meet ups still happen, they are a cheap and local way to be face to face.

Also, maybe local small business? In the same way that you found the pizzeria, is there maybe a local chain of dentist offices or veterinarians or something? Corporate hiring is totally broken, but "finding good people" is still a top problem, especially for medium sized business (50-100 employees, 5-10 locations, across 2-3 states).

Can you get a shitty IT ops job that can beat the pizzeria salary? And help repair your resume hole?

Best wishes.


I was unemployed for 8 months a few years ago and I filled the gap with work on my own platform which I listed as my startup. Unfortunately, I couldn't find any users for it but it served its purpose as a filler. I got a job with a different startup in an area which I didn't enjoy and against my principles but beggars can't be choosers and so I managed to last 8 months by faking enthusiasm. Still, the founder was quite impressive in some ways and I learned a lot from observing his behavior. That job served as an on-ramp to a truly horrible software job which I hated; codebase was legacy and over-engineered and pay was low... But that job became an on-ramp to my current job which is consulting. Boring subject matter but has a strong AI focus and quite challenging. There were a lot of issues with that job. It's been a real struggle but the leaders are reasonable, well connected and it's a good area.


I don’t have much to offer here, outside of an abundance of sympathy and well-wishes.

I have a job now, but I have had long periods of unemployment in the past, also with about 15 years of experience. Hope you find something soon.


Firstly, I deeply empathize with your situation and its important to note the market is historically really bad for everyone right now.

After 15 years of experience, you should have people you can instantly call who can get you interviews or even direct jobs at the place they are working.

The idea of applying to jobs after 10 years of experience is very futile. At that point, your network and industry reputation gets you directly placed.

Your peers (the people you started your career with) with the same YOE are in hiring/leadership roles now like head of engineering, VP, Staff Engineer etc. so calling them and asking to be directly placed is the way.


This may be true for some but just to provide a counterpoint: I have 25 YoE and this year changed jobs twice, both times just using normal application channels eg applying directly to Linkedin jobs. I got plenty of interviews and managed to get hired both times so it's definitely possible to do it this way.


Find an early stage company that is doing something you are interested in, email the founder or early employee and ask to buy them a coffee and talk shop.

Find one that has an open source product and contribute

Organize a hackathon or conference and invite people to speak.

Go into a random small business and tell them you are looking for problems in a business that can be solved with software and you’d like to build something for them for free if they are willing to let you shadow them.

Within a month or two of putting yourself in the center of connections, especially if you give value without expecting anything in return, you find there are a lot of people that need help building things.


This might not be something you like, especially for a veteran SWE, who’s good with indivitual contributions or work with independent teams.

However, if you are willing, there is a massive demand for SWE who have been dirty with codes for ages, can talk to customers, and `manage / work with` young and upcoming Indian engineers (both in the US and India).

Many enterprises are struggling to find people in the venn diagram of engineering + communication/translation of business to technology and back to business on what the technology meant in business language.


if you don't want SWE then your best bet is to go back to school to do masters(or some trade) and do TA on a side. This will take care of the gap as well as get you full school resources to find connections and new opportunities.

If you want to stick to SWE:

1. you will have more luck with startups. Go to local startup events, there will be plenty of non-technical founders, they always need help.

2. start building projects so you can fill in the gap in the resume, doesn't matter how big or small as long as you ship something. There is always a creative way to describe a gap in employment that doesn't have to be a lie but you need to show something

3. find freelance recruiter(not part of the company but runs own recruiting company or something), they have way more flow of jobs going through them and they can directly make someone look at your resume


I think I would advice against masters because there are so many masters on the market. It doesn’t really stand out.


Yeah, for whatever reason, hiring managers and recruiters are incredibly suspicious of people who aren't working at present.

I have a buddy who was a quant for a decade, but took a few years off to raise kids, and he found it incredibly difficult to get back in.


solid advice here - as someone who hires SWE's often. interesting,fun and creative personal and public github projects get my attention over any bullet on a resume


For what it’s worth, I recently switched to electro mechanic at an about 100 man company. I used to be software engineer and have a PhD. I’m very happy about the switch. They say I’m learning quickly plus I automated a bunch of stuff for the head mechanics as well. It’s quite tough work from time to time but the relaxed down to earth colleagues and the mix with more physical labor - feeling more rewarding - easily make up for it.


I was thinking about applying for an apprenticeship. My job as a sysadmin is relatively safe for now but who knows for how long.

It would be an apprenticeship as industrial electric technician specialised in power distribution plants at the local TSO. I would be done in two years instead of the usual 3.5...


Honestly go to tech meetups or social events/groups that are popular with techies in your area. They have to be things you'd enjoy at some level.

Make friends, ask them about themselves, their work, if they like it there, tell them you are job hunting after stepping back from a former role before layoffs happened.

Also if there's wealthy non profits near you, see if you can volunteer a few hours as a consultant, that way you have recent things you've done.


That is so tough. I'm sorry to hear that

What have you tried?

Like others said the way in is often who you know. Ask your network for help, referrals. Tell them what you are looking for. People often get jobs thru weak ties. Your network probably won't hire you, but someone you know, knows someone who is hiring.

If you're considering a local pizzeria, taking a break from full time search and working as a SWE contractor could also be an option to get your foot in the door. Companies hire contractors to full time. And it probably pays at least what you'd make at the pizza shop

And make sure you have a good story about your gap. You took time to heal after xyz, time to focus on family, time to start a business, time to help a family member, etc. people understand that and respect it. But if you have no story then they assume the worst ie you've been unhirable


Look for a staffing agency like AppleOne or another reputable agency that has established relationships with different companies.

This is what worked for me. After working for the same company for about 14 years, my team was outsourced. I was laid off a couple of months before the pandemic. I decided to give entrepreneurship a try, started my business and worked as an IT consultant, but after landing only a few clients and paying so much in taxes and insurance, I realized I needed to return to the workforce.

The challenge was that potential employers could see my situation in one of two ways: either I had failed at running my own business, or I had a gap in my employment history of about 2 yrs.

After going through several interviews directly with companies and not landing a position, I decided to take a different approach. I went through a staffing agency with the goal of getting my foot in the door as a temporary employee or contractor. My thinking was that once a company had the opportunity to see my skills, experience, and work ethic firsthand, I would have a better chance of being hired permanently.

And that's exactly what happened! Thank God, after six months as a contractor, I was offered a permanent position.


"In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE."

Well, why? Wouldn't severance have been better and ride it out to the end?

Easy wins would be to change location on linkedin and see what different regions of the USA have for you, not exactly relocate, but atleast get the funnel primed.


Copy and paste from another comment:

had savings, was really tired of the company, it had no vision, people I have worked with and imagined that quitting + finding job in the early 2025(market was completely different 2y ago, at least I though so), will be a lot faster than sitting there awaiting of being canned, which is soul crushing after witnessing two layoffs, mostly likely getting canned, which is another hit and then start looking for the job. i.e "proactive" > sitting & waiting. The severance package was negligible - $2w-1m.


If you had gotten laid off you would have been eligible for unemployment benefits, right? and you could have start job hunting while working at the other place?


I'm sure there's things that they could have done better in retrospect. They know that.

They said they didn't expect finding a new job to be so hard


In addition to what everyone has mentioned, I'd spend some time learning a new language or two (JS, Python, SQL, whatever you feel like that's on the popular side).


When I have been laid off I have always created an LLC and gotten a business license and did minor consulting. In Virginia, you can start an LLC completely online for like $70, get your FEIN from the IRS for free if I remember correctly, and $30 for a business license for the city. About $100 and you get no gap, and look entreprenurial while you are it it.


I tried doing that. Recruiters immediately want to know for whom I worked as independent and in the conversations where I said that I did independent work like developing websites for the clients, recruiters immediately hang up on me. They all want to see me working for a bigger client.

If you have a better way to formulate "I'm independent contractor", I would like to hear that.


My self-employment via LLC is a bit eccentric in that I've done both software development and construction/property services (licensed general contractor) through the same company. I have observed more interest in my resume when I put my title as "Owner|Software Developer" rather than something like "Consultant".


tell them you signed an NDA. 2 years unemployed but with 15 years of prior experience and you are fine


What's your value proposition? What do you do better than other candidates? What excites you enough to go deep, understand thoroughly, and build something others can't build? I can't speak to the value of coding, but engineering is always in high demand... what do you engineer?


This year, I got two good, serious opportunities (no spam, personal) simply by talking to people about things I work on, without even looking for a job. The one thing that strikes me from your write-up is that you barely mention what you are actually capable of or what your expertise is, but you are "size-dropping" your former employers. Who cares how many employees these companies had?

> I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI

This is the only skills thing you wrote in your post, and that's telling me so much.

So, who are you? Why should anyone hire you? Do you think you sound like someone who has something to offer with that kind of statement?

Just figure out who you are and dedicate all your time to proving that, and opportunities will show up.

I am not trying to be rude or offend you, but I think you need this more than someone comforting you. You obviously have potential, but why don't you talk about that potential and stay strong? Nobody hires out of pity. This HN post was just another missed opportunity.

Show people what you can actually do and be confident. Then talk every day to someone out there who works in your area of expertise, and opportunities will come.


This sounds a lot like the pep talk you would give to an aspiring actor or researcher - or any hyper competitive field where the vast majority fail and success is the exception for the exceptional.

This is the complete opposite of a job market in stable equilibrium where the quality of an experienced applicant from another large firm is by definition sufficient to clear the minimum bar, the only thing remaining being to negotiate exact compensation.

Software is now the kind of field where you need another day job to survive while you polish your craft and industry contacts.


3y/25yoe for me so clearly I have no advice to give, just want to say that it's not you, it's a terrible state of affair out there right now.


Well,you both could be building something really amazing in one or two years (content, SaaS, startup, small business ... ). Self employed is a way to go for many of us, but i´m not US based, don't know how hard it is there.


Whelp this is probably the wrong thread to be reading :(

It’s good to remember I’m not special, I suppose: in a bad way or a good way.


> In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.

Just curious, was there a severance package?

Why was it a good idea to quit without lining up another job first?

I am not being critical, just want to understand your thought process.

I don't think a resume gap matters... I've got gaps on mine. I can explain them if asked.


This jumped out at me too. Why would you proactively quit a job because there was a rumored layoff? If you don’t get laid off, great you have a job. If you do get laid off, you probably get severance and unemployment. Sometimes other “perks” like getting medical coverage for some time. This is months of expenses.


had savings, was really tired of the company, it had no vision, people I have worked with and imagined that quitting + finding job in the early 2025, will be a lot faster than sitting there awaiting of being canned, which is soul crushing after witnessing two layoffs, mostly likely getting canned, which is another hit and then start looking for the job. i.e "proactive" > sitting & waiting. The severance package was negligible - $2w-1m.


> Just curious, was there a severance package?

As far as I know, no. Std. - month or two weeks (I don't remember, exact, but short). Before that, they had two rounds of layoff, both happened just before thanksgiving (this time of the year..) and it was brutal to observe from the sidelines.

> Why was it a good idea to quit without lining up another job first?

Hindsight, f@&# no. It was terrible mistake. I was thinking finding another position will piece of cake.

>I don't think a resume gap matters... I've got gaps on mine. I can explain them if asked.

Oh, I did it and it is immediately a show stopper. Maybe I should frame my gap some other way.


Resume gaps matter to an ATS if you are looking for a job now, because your competition (either real - people laid off recently - or fake - there’s boatloads of resume fraud in the last few years) doesn’t have those gaps and the software will rank them higher.

Sure, those gaps are easy to explain (and perfectly reasonable in the current climate) to a human, the challenge is to get in front of said human in the first place.


What do you say about gaps? I'm coming up on a year and starting to have recruiters ask what's going on. Idk what to say. For whatever reason I can't convert interviews to a job.


Glibly, that they're asking the wrong person.

It's their own damn fault for contributing to the crazy state of hiring.

Tell them to speak to Altman et al and ask them to explain this crazy world we're in right now.

Good luck my friend


So Sorry to hear it. I can understand how you are feeling. I went through something similar during covid. Try in cloud computing, AWS or Azure, they have roles which pays well. I can help you with the referral if you need one.


I've realized that my traditional job sources have decayed in quality, and that it's possible to spend all day every day applying for positions I'm qualified for but wouldn't enjoy at companies that will never call me back. I've also realized that aggressive filtering still leaves me with more postings than I can seriously apply to.

Adding a "value" dimension to things like job sources, descriptions, and application processes helped quite a bit. For example, an external freelance recruiter cold-calling me would be low-value while an internal recruiter I have a previous relationship with would be higher. Using a service to process applications, requiring a Linkedin profile, leetcode in their interviews, company size, and so forth. I'm enumerating and ranking the red flags I've run into based on time spent and result. All geared towards eliminating contact with the sort of person who cares about a gap in your resume because they will waste my time.

Non-tech related job postings reduce the same way if you understand the flags in their domain. Are you applying to jobs that want you to think inside a box? Job posts that exist only as a legal requirement? Roles that come with an assumption of age? If you're overqualified does that benefit your employer or introduce problems?


This is going to sound harsh to any developer or "code artisan" reading this but you have two paths:

- you find a way to work for yourself which means figuring out distribution which takes time and money

- you find a different line of work. it might be labor it might be talking witih people it might be working with your hands but it wont be the same comfortable software development anymore.

Software is solved. Stop looking for the same job you've been working on for the past decade. They are not hiring anymore and if they do they have no plan on keeping you once they figure out a way for someone cheaper to use AI to do your job.

They don't care about your opinions on different languages or frameworks. The people that are looking to hire are trying to figure out how you can teach Indian developers to use AI effectively.


> Software is solved.

Software has practically torched its reputation to the ground in the last month, let alone over the last year. Outage after outage, outrage after outrage. We've disrupted the lives of hundreds of thousands of people (hell, if not millions) in the last two weeks.

But I know as I write this: there is no mountain of proof high enough to change the opinion of anyone who thinks software is "solved". AI is the irrefutable hypothesis.


Your parent is arguing what execs have been convinced of, not necessarily an obvious objective truth.

AI is finding bugs that have been in PHP, Java, Ruby, NginX for years or decades. Even if "software isn't solved", AI is going to be a big part of the solution.

I think the parent's comment is better read "anybody is capable of creating an app / SaaS these days, so distribution / marketing and the idea for the product are more important than implementation." This seems to be what the zeitgeist of solopreneurs are telling each other.


This isn’t true even at a cursory glance. We would be hearing this constantly if this was the case. People wouldn’t be “anxious” and “worried” about AI or whatever but would be talking about how to make ends meet instead of their existential feelings.

So you took the opportunity of someone asking a personal and important question to spread generic FUD. Despicable.


the question is how long do we have to wait until the guys that think like this get fired or get sued into bankruptcy.

it’s an attrition game, we have to keep building small software that works, doesn’t get hacked and doesn’t go down while these accelerationists 100x into their crash.


I hate to be the one to tell you this but this fantasy is not happening. The industry has changed and it's going to continue on this trajectory so you have to learn how to do this well. There are going to be companies popping up that will claim to have figured out how to build with these agents quickly, securely and in a manner that's maintainable. Those are the companies that will take our jobs. So either learn how to build like them or move on.


> I hate to be the one to tell you this but this

One would expect a phrase like that to lead into fresh factual information, not a subjective (however possibly well-informed) prediction arguing a point very similar to the one they were contesting in the first place.


> so you have to learn how to do this well.

I get that you believe that agent development is good, but why are you trying to convince me to join? for my own good? or is it cultish

even if you assume vibecoding is revolutionary, there’s still going to be an oversupply of vibecoders, and virgin programmers are going to be quite rare, in fact it’s already happening

vibeocders lose capacity to go back to actually writing and reading code, and the vibecoding force is composed of non technical folk, and technical folk alike. Technical folk degrade their experience by coalescing skillsets

And I just haven’t seen a big leap in software, maybe lots of vulns are discovered? Vibecoding still hasn’t brought anything major like Chatgpt, wikipedia, uber, iphone, just slop and cves


Consider working in other countries? any job in a tech or any company is good for you at this moment. You can move to development afterward. Also consider moving to other cities to find work.


I have family, home and a lot of connections. I can't just uproot my entire existence for a job. US market is pretty big and I live, smack in the middle of the major metropolitan area, not far away from DC.


Have you tried putting a profile on Upwork? I know it mostly has a reputation as an "offshoring" site, but the globalisation of employment has flattened wages somewhat -- that is to say that disparity between what you pay for a good freelancer in Pakistan ($35 - $50) compared with a decent freelancer in the US is ($60 - $100) is not as great as it once was.

Like you might not be able to earn a full senior software engineering rate right away, but you can probably make more per hour than you would at a pizzeria and you can work irregular hours (ie. you could do both). This would also give you exposure potentially to new tech and/or skills and would give you some reviews that you could show to recruiters.


Change your location might be a good start. Not many companies do remote, and most software stuff is in bay area.


I was just in the same boat as you; same length of unemployment and tech stack. We've already depleted some of our savings while also dealing with a tenant who hasn't paid their rent this year. But a couple months ago, I got a job doing Coding Evaluation & Training Data via an outsourcing company[1]. It isn't coding per se but I do get to use my full stack experience QA'ing AI. Not glamorous and feels a bit odd training my AI overload but I set my hours and get paid decently.

For more info on this alternative path, you can read some recent media coverage[2]

[1] https://wayfinders.tech

[2] https://www.cbsnews.com/news/will-ai-take-my-job-60-minutes-...


Same but 4 YOE. Left due to personal reasons but am having difficulties getting a job. If you can swing it, working on a personal project like many have suggested and maybe even transitioning it to a startup can be a good way to practice development with AI. Otherwise its just a numbers game I hope. Fingers crossed for you!


DO NOT QUIT.

Try something small, read and understand economics. Understand the human relationship money, and you can figure out a way to earn and keep earning.


The person in that position has limited time. Understanding human relationships can take ages, and I think it's not a good practical advice. It's a hard problem unfortunately, especially if the market is unstable.


> and learned the AI

AI subs are becoming a requirement in 2026. Learn to "wield a harness" and treat it as an engineering problem.

See a company you like? Build something for them. It's the quickest way to get noticed


And then have them steal your idea, dont give you a job, and put you on a blackball list.

Dont do this. Build something for yourself, sure, but dont do this.


I would have thought this was jaded

until I was recently ghosted by a company after two interviews, including one with the owner, and had followed up with a few weeks of marketing material.

I wonder what they’ll do afterward.

BUILD SOMETHING FOR YOURSELF!


Consider widening the scope of where you look. For example, instead of pure SWE or even SRE roles maybe consider an IT role. That's what I had to do. Do I like it as much? No. Does it pay as much? No. Does it pay my bills? Yes.


Consider working for yourself. It's easy to start an LLC, and cheap. Professional insurance and bonding is, or has been, pretty cheap. If you want to secure your future, sometimes you have to do it yourself.


Maybe the real people are getting laid off, but their application page is flooded with spambots and liars who claim to not be laid off. And to the eyes of an ATS, those people are the ones who get in front of a human (even if ultimately they are fake).


Getting laid off isn’t the problem, the problem is that you couldn’t get hired for two years. You need to explain that.


Stigma, or maybe heuristic. "We don't want to hire somebody nobody else would hire." It's silly, since you could just evaluate for yourself, but a lot of judgements are silly.


I'd been looking since March. What worked for me:

1. Message all your contacts on linkedin. Just say hi how's it going etc. Got a job offer straight back from one. Another told me he was leaving his role and he could put me forward. I ended up taking this

2. Upload CV to job sites. Had 2 decent companies find me this way

3. If you see a job you like try to call or email the recruiter directly and skip the job boards

As everyone else has said, recruitment is broken. Go to meetups, whatever. You need to do personal networking.


my last few positions were from people messaging one mailing list i was on or another, asking if anyone wants to join their team

keep checking that junk folder :)


public sector work in lower cost of living areas or "second tier" tech hubs like Salt Lake, Nashville, Dallas etc.

When people with fairly successful CVs end up in this situation I always wonder if they genuinely apply everywhere because there's plenty of employment open in the public sector, healthcare and basically everything outside "Fortune 50+".

Lower cost of living areas and mid-sized cities in the US have still pretty high demand for IT workers and usually not 50 people running through the door competing for the same job


- while i dont have the experience of your kind (big companies and all)

- i have been unemployed for 10 yrs now due to disabilities


I think increasingly the answer is to accept that the game is up. We are Detroit auto workers in 1985. The old world is gone and it's not coming back. You will probably never again make what you used to. My advice would be to find something real and hard to do that people need done, and you might be able to earn a living. Fortunately software developers are well positioned to be able to do this; adapting and figuring things out is our whole thing.


> We are Detroit auto workers in 1985

Interesting framing and wondering about the productive outcome of the world’s best autoworker of the past 40 years. What kind of living did that achieve?


Embrace AI and see what you can do with it that you never considered. Time for a moonshot. Build tools you always wanted. Solve a problem for someone in your life. While there aren’t many jobs, there are just as many, if not more, problems to get after.

This might lead to a job.


This is terrible advice for the commoner who already burnt through their savings and is considering working in a pizza joint. (Also, outside of the AI psychosis, it turns out AI only speeds up part of the product development process, and it takes much more than just software development to get to a stage where a product pays the bills).


What should you do? Lie.

I’ve been on both sides of the job search in the past couple years. Like you, absolutely no luck with cold applications.

On the hiring side, opening a position got me a thousand of applications per day, all ChatGPT’d resumes from monkeys who likely couldn’t engineer their way out of a wet paper bag (beyond just grossly lying about experience, there’s also actual remote work fraud, either from the “overemployed” crowd if not outright scams or North Koreans). Unfortunately, in all that mess I’m sure there were really good legitimate candidates but there is no way for me to tell without talking to them, which was impossible considering the sheer scale of the spam onslaught.

My advice is twofold. 1) Lie - nobody legitimate would actually care about your 2-year career gap, yet due to the scale of the spam, automated tools have to be used to cull the incoming firehose, and those unfortunately do care. So lie and extend your last job, or make up some consulting gig, or whatever floats your boat. As long as you can walk the talk during the interview, you are good. As a hirer I couldn’t care less (and wouldn’t even have any reason to dig too deep) if you are otherwise competent and able to talk about your work and can demonstrate you are a good developer and not just a dumbass vibecoder ticket-mover. In the sea of shit we’re currently swimming, even a candidate I know is lying is fine as long as they’re otherwise competent.

2) cold applications are pretty much dead due to the aforementioned spam problem. So my recommendation is to polish up your LinkedIn (you do have 15 YOE of real experience after all, with people you worked with and stuff) and then reach out to strategic people at prospective companies. Don’t even ask for a job to begin with - offer consultancy, etc (the danger of asking for a job straight away is that they shut down the conversation and redirect you to the cold application page - a dead end). The point is to have a conversation with a human, to demonstrate you are a real person and not an idiot with a spambot. If the conversation goes anywhere you’ve just fast-tracked the whole bullshit application process (you might still be asked to submit it, but at that point it’s merely a formality and you’ve already got a contact that will follow up internally to make sure your application goes somewhere).

Also, if you’re at the stage where you’re considering a blue-collar job, target companies that could potentially benefit from IT skills or where you can use them to make your job easier if not make their job easier and get promoted that way. In a sense, you’re using the blue-collar job merely as a foot in the door to be able to show up and talk to people. While it’s unlikely this would yield good pay right away (and potentially not ever), it’s a good way to build connections and potentially get something done (remember that those companies don’t get IT people and might be stuck with a shitty MSP handling their IT. Having someone “good with computers” internally would be a godsend for them and a win-win situation).

Ultimately in the age of AI-assisted spam and no consequences for fraud, the hardest part is getting a respectable human connection. Lie (within reason) if you have to, to achieve that, then be yourself, and you’ll get somewhere.

Good luck!

URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/19/stock-market-today-live-updates.html, See on Hacker News

Stocks tumble Friday

The three leading U.S. indexes experienced a massive sell-off on Friday.

The S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, while the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28% to 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33.

— Sean Conlon

'Risk is to the downside' when below the 200-day moving average, BTIG says

All three major averages were trading below their 200-day moving averages on Friday, and BTIG believes more turmoil could be ahead.

"Generally speaking once something is below a 200 DMA, the risk is to the downside," said Jonathan Krinsky, the firm's chief market technician.

Thursday marked the sixth consecutive day of declines for the S&P 500, and Krinsky found that over the last 30 years, there are only three prior instances of six-day losing streaks that close below the 200-day moving average but not by more than 3%.

"The 'slightly' good news is that all three saw SPX higher five days later. The not so good news is that all of them saw meaningful downside after that small pop," he said.

When assessing Thursday's performance, Wolfe Research found that the broad market index's "violent" reversal after its attempt to move back to its 200-day moving average at the open was succeeded by the "worst breadth reading" since last December, seeing decliners outnumber advancers by 12:1.

"Broken trends and deteriorating momentum remain significant headwinds," wrote technical analyst Rob Ginsberg in a Thursday note. "The bulls need to mount a powerful defense here to stabilize the market and begin reversing the broader deterioration."

— Sean Conlon

Gas prices fall ahead of Thanksgiving, but remain above last year

A customer purchases gas at a station on September 15, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.

Scott Olson | Getty Images

The national average for regular gasoline fell to $3.69 a gallon on Friday, down from $3.72 on Thursday, according to AAA. Prices are still about 59 cents higher than a year ago.

The drop comes ahead of Thanksgiving next week, with 73 million people expected to take road trips. 

"It's possible the national average will drop another 15 cents by next Thursday and avoid setting a new record," according to AAA's post.

Brent ​crude futures, the international benchmark, were up 0.64% to $92.57 a barrel on Friday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December rose 0.93% to settle at $83.98 a barrel.

Brent and WTI prices - YTD

— Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells

Humana upgraded to buy at TD Cowen

In this photo illustration, the Humana Inc. logo is displayed on a smartphone screen.

Rafael Henrique | SOPA Images | Lightrocket | Getty Images

Humana shares rose 3% after TD Cowen upgraded the healthcare services company to buy from hold, raising the price target to $485, implying a 28% upside from the stock's Thursday close of $380.

Humana - YTD

"Taking into account 2026 performance, 2027 Medicare Advantage benefit design and 2028 Stars results, we see a relatively clear path towards a meaningful step-up in 2027 EPS growth and more than $40 EPS in 2028," the bank said in its note.

Adjusted EPS estimates for 2026, 2027, and 2028 remain unchanged at $9.51, $18.41, and $40.42, respectively.

— Deena Zaidi

Anthropic tops Vanguard's retail investor trading charts in debut

Daniela Amodei, co-founder and president of Anthropic PBC, center left, and Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic PBC, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026.

Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.

Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.

Vanguard said about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.

To be sure, Vanguard said a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.

Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.

— Alex Harring

BTIG's Krinsky says technicals show the sell-off isn't over yet

BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.

He specifically noted Apple, the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he said. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now."

He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.

Krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.

Apple vs. S&P 500 1 month.

— Davis Giangiulio

Anthropic debut underperforms other blockbuster IPOs

CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei inside the Nasdaq MarketSite ahead of the anticipated IPO of artificial intelligence company Anthropic in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Charly Triballeau | Afp | Getty Images

Anthropic shares gave back much of that advance on Friday, falling more than 12% in afternoon trading.

— Sean Conlon

Trump wants to ban U.S. companies from building data centers abroad

US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio listen as US President Donald Trump speaks during a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Nov. 20, 2026.

Ken Cedeno | Afp | Getty Images

President Donald Trump said on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.

"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here."

He added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.

— Kevin Breuninger and Davis Giangiulio

VIX volatility index climbs above 30, up as much as 13% intraday

The VIX volatility index, a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose another 13% intraday Friday to 32.27, after jumping as much as 16% Thursday, according to FactSet data.

The VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has now risen for six of the past seven days. The index hasn't closed above 30 since late March.

The VIX in November

— Scott Schnipper

Fed Governor Cook warns about falling behind on inflation

Lisa Cook, governor of the US Federal Reserve, during the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR) Policy Forum at Stanford University in Stanford, California, US, on Wednesday, May 27, 2026.

David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook expressed caution about the dangers posed by inflation, saying Friday that if the central bank doesn't act now it risks having to do more later.

"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook said in remarks delivered in Chile.

"Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she added. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households."

Cook was one of only two FOMC members who voted against the pause. Markets strongly expect the committee to approve a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.

— Jeff Cox

Tech sector heads for worst week since April 2025

The tech selling intensified in late-morning trading, with the sector down more than 5% on the day. That decline pushed its week-to-date losses to 10.5% as of 11:57 a.m. ET. That would be tech's biggest one-week drop since April 4, 2025, when the Trump administration announced massive tariffs on imported products.

XLK year to date

— Fred Imbert

Nasdaq Composite turns negative for 2026

The Nasdaq Composite dropped Friday, turning negative for 2026, as even Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings failed to revive the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy index was last lower by 2.6% for the trading session, falling slightly on the year.

Nasdaq Composite, 1-day

— Sarah Min

Bitcoin breaks below $60,000 for the first time since July

Bitcoin signage in Times Square in New York, Dec. 9, 2025.

Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Bitcoin slid more than 4% with the broader market, falling below the $60,000 level for the first time since July.

The flagship cryptocurrency was last trading at $59,554.95 and is now heading for a retest its July low of $57,737.35.

Bitcoin, 1-day

Ether fell 6% to $1,650.79, its lowest level since July 2.

— Tanaya Macheel

Consumer sentiment reading moves higher as inflation outlook improves sharply

A woman shops at a store in New York, the United States, Nov. 4, 2026.

Zhang Fengguo | Xinhua News Agency | Getty Images

The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday.

The survey's headline sentiment index rose to 51.5, up 7.3% from a month ago and exactly in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate.

Inflation expectations at the one-year horizon declined sharply, down to 3.7%, which was a full percentage point below a month ago and well below the mid-month November reading of 4.3%. This was the lowest reading since March. The five-year outlook slipped to 3.3%.

"Despite the softening in inflation expectations, consumers continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation—rather than unemployment—will cause greater hardship for consumers in the next one or two years," survey director Joanne Hsu said.

— Jeff Cox

The recent losses in tech stocks and the S&P 500 'have further to run,' says Capital Economics

The recent pressure seen in technology stocks as well as the S&P 500 may not be over yet, according to James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics.

"The success of Anthropic's IPO yesterday as other AI-related stocks tumbled highlights how different parts of the AI ecosystem no longer move as one," he wrote in a Friday note. "We think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run — and how this plays out within the stock market will depend on what is driving these falls."

Reilly believes the S&P 500 index should fall to 6,500 by the end of next year. The index closed at 7,175.83 on Thursday.

— Sean Conlon

Stocks open lower

The three major averages were trading in the red on Friday morning.

The Nasdaq Composite declined 1.3% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 moved down 0.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 48 points, or 0.1%.

— Sean Conlon

Seaport is ‘cautious’ on Anthropic after its record-smashing IPO

People walk past a billboard advertising the artificial intelligence company Anthropic in Times Square on its initial public offering (IPO) day in New York City on Nov. 19, 2026.

Leonardo Munoz | AFP | Getty Images

Anthropic made its historic Wall Street debut on Thursday. But one research firm is taken a cautious stance on the stock.

Seaport Research initiated coverage of the artificial intelligence stock with a neutral rating. 

"Anthropic is an incredible company, but it is also asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors," analyst Jay Goldberg said in a note. "We think the company will need time to grow into its valuation and answer some very big questions about its growth trajectory. We are not negative on the company, but we are cautious."

CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here.

— Liz Napolitano

Anthropic, Ross Stores and Intuit among the stocks making moves before the bell

  • Anthropic: The stock was down more than 9%, a day after the AI giant made its public market debut. The stock rallied 17% on Thursday, though it closed well below its highs of the session.
  • Ross Stores: Shares fell 5% as the discount retailer's forecast disappointed traders.
  • Intuit: Shares slid roughly 8% in premarket trading after the financial software company cut its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook, citing a slowdown at Credit Karma.

Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making premarket moves.

— Deena Zaidi, Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert

VIX rises above 30

The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) was trading above 30 on Friday morning as the selling pressure on U.S. equity futures ramped up.

The index, also known as Wall Street's "fear gauge," was last at 30.99, reaching its highest level since March.

VIX, 1-day

— Sean Conlon

Ubisoft drops 14% as outlook disappoints

On Jan. 9, Ubisoft said it was postponing the launch of "Assassin's Creed Shadows" and had appointed advisors to review strategic options.

Ina Fassbender | AFP via Getty Images

Shares of French video game publisher Ubisoft fell 13.2% in European morning trade, after the maker of the "Assassin's Creed" franchise forecast net bookings of around 250 million euros ($274 million) for the October to December period.

That was below a 361 million euro consensus estimate cited by analysts at TD Cowen and represents a fall from 338 million euros in the same quarter last year, at a time when hype in the market is being dominated by the launch of Take-Two's "Grand Theft Auto VI". Ubisoft cited a "particularly crowded holiday season" in its outlook.

Ubisoft on Thursday also reported net bookings down 16.5% year-on-year in its fiscal first half, with second-quarter net bookings of 389 million euros, above its guidance of around 370 million euros.

Ubisoft share price.

— Jenni Reid

Treasury yields are sharply lower as investors flee to safe havens

U.S. Treasury yields fell on Friday, as an equities sell-off drove investors into safe-haven assets ahead of Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's speech later in the session.

The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, loans and credit card debt — was down 6 basis points at 4.989%.

The 2-year Treasury note yield, more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was also 6 basis points lower at 4.713%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield – which moves on wider geopolitical developments – was down 4 basis points at 5.361%.

— Natalie Feary

U.S. tech giants tumble in premarket; global chip firms down

Premarket moves point to continued downward momentum in Big Tech, including Anthropic, which is seen 6% lower at 4:25 a.m. ET after its blockbuster debut.

Nvidia slipped 1.9% in premarket with the stock at its lowest level in more than a year following a rollercoaster period. Among other Mag 7 stocks, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon and Tesla dipped into the red, while Apple nudged 0.5% higher.

Semiconductor stocks fell, with Broadcom down 3%, AMD losing 4.95% and Micron shedding 3.8%.

European chip players ASML and ASM International dropped 5.8% and 5.4%, respectively. That came after Japanese semiconductor stocks tumbled during Friday trade, with Tokyo Electron closing 7.06% lower, Lasertec shedding 9.21% and Renesas Electronics losing 7.02%.

— Jenni Reid

No market can weather a proper unwind of the tech trade: investment strategist

Bénédicte Lowe, equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, told CNBC there was a "mind-boggling" disconnect in the fact that a market sell-off has coincided with the biggest-ever IPO in Anthropic — but that investors were "panic selling" as they try to gauge whether AI sentiment has peaked.

The sell-off is now in a second leg in which investors are even ditching traditionally defensive plays in a broad risk-off environment, she said. Tech worries are seeping into sectors such as FTSE 100 mining companies, hit by fears of a recession.

"No market can weather a proper unwind of the tech trade," Lowe said.

Any upside going into year-end will require a stabilization of the tech story and market moves, she added.

— Natalie Feary and Jenni Reid

Highly rated corporates is where 'everyone is going to park their money,' analyst says

Matthias Reschke, head of European Investment Grade Finance for JP Morgan, told "Squawk Box Europe" that corporate spreads are looking "very resilient" in the wake of the equity market sell-off, though the market is "much more nervous than it used to be."

With risk appetite down across markets and spreads widening, even for investment-grade corporates, he said this is where he expects "everyone is going to park their money."

The big question is if inflation will come down next year, he added. Reschke expects persistent inflation pressures, meaning government 10-year yields may "remain elevated for a while."

— Natalie Feary

European stocks open lower, joining global tech sell-off

European stocks fell at Friday's open, with the benchmark Stoxx 600 index down 0.83% after hitting a four week-low on Thursday.

The region's technology stocks joined the global sell-off, last down 2.7%, with chip stocks ASML, ASM International and Be Semiconductor among the worst performers.

Stoxx 600 index.

— Jenni Reid

'Lot of upside' in AI stocks despite growing market skepticism, Anthropic investor says

The market is skeptical about "all layers of the AI layer cake" but that can be a "great setup for investors," Brett Winton, chief futurist at ARK Investment Management who has Anthropic in all his portfolios, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

A key worry is that the huge R&D spend of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX will generate sufficient returns, he said.

"The market really thinks that Anthropic's revenue per gigawatt of compute has essentially peaked and is only going to go down from here. And the history and the returns they've got to their training suggest exactly the opposite, where they already have amazing gross margins," he said.

"What they're getting is the ability to serve more intelligence per GPU [graphics processing unit] that they use, and as they deliver on that, they're able to monetize per gigawatt of GPU more successfully... That's why you've seen Anthropic's growth margins expand as quickly as they have, even as their top line has been explosively growing. So we think that's going to continue."

On concerns about the infrastructure buildout around AI, Winton said people increasingly doubted whether companies will be willing to pay for the compute they're delivering to market.

"We take exactly the opposite view. So the overall market for knowledge workers we think is a $40 trillion market for AI software selling into the knowledge workforce, and so there's plenty of room to run if collectively Anthropic and OpenAI are only annualizing revenue on the order of $150 billion per year right now."

"So we're really in the earliest, earliest stages of what will be a really dynamic game, and we think there's a lot of upside from here."

— Jenni Reid

SoftBank sees worst day in over two years as AI sell-off hits Asia

Pedestrians walk past signage outside the building where the SoftBank Group headquarters is located in Tokyo on Nov. 11, 2025.

Kazuhiro Nogi | AFP | Getty Images

Shares in Japan's SoftBank Group closed 14.48% lower on Friday, their worst day since August 2024, as a broader sell-off swept through Asian technology stocks.

The decline highlights investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.

The group is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival. Read more.

— Jenny Lee

Asia-Pacific markets ended sharply lower as tech sell-off sweeps the region

Asia-Pacific markets ended sharply lower on Friday as a sweeping sell-off in technology stocks dragged major indexes across the region into negative territory.

Japan's Nikkei 225 plunged 5.06% to close at 56,436.65, while the Topix dropped 3.88% to 3,674.22.

South Korea's Kospi sank 5.21% to close at 4,869.96, while the small-cap Kosdaq shed 5.71% to 645.68.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed at 8,592.6.

Mainland China's CSI 300 slipped 0.76% to 3,954.57, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down 2.24% in its final hour of trading.

— Jenny Lee

UK retail sales beat forecasts

Shoppers walk past the window display for the United Colors of Benetton store on Oxford Street where a 70% clearance sale is on, on 13th October 2026, in London, England.

Richard Baker | In Pictures | Getty Images

British retail sales volumes rose by 0.7% in October, the country's Office for National Statistics said Friday, continuing a choppy trend following a 0.6% decline in September and 0.8% gain in August.

The monthly figure was better than the flat reading forecast in a Reuters poll.

Retail activity was boosted over the summer by the soccer World Cup, while analysts expected weakening consumer sentiment and higher U.K. inflation to weigh on activity.

Traders continue to expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates by 25 basis points in December, though the odds of a hike have fallen to around 80% from 90% a week ago, according to money market pricing on LSEG.

— Jenni Reid

Gold hits more than 1-year low as sell-off deepens

FILE PHOTO: 24 karat gold bars are seen at the United States West Point Mint facility in West Point, New York June 5, 2013.

Shannon Stapleton | Reuters

Spot gold fell 2.81% to $3,520.05 per ounce on Friday, putting the precious metal on track for its worst weekly decline in eight months, according to Reuters.

Bullion, which hit its lowest since September 2025, has lost about 8.9% this week, according to LSEG data, pressured by a stronger U.S. dollar and growing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December.

Gold futures declined 4.55% to $3,519.20, a fresh 52-week low.

— Jenny Lee

Taiwan stocks head for worst weekly drop in nearly three decades

Taiwan's benchmark Taiex fell 5.65% on Friday, bringing its weekly losses to 14.89%, its steepest weekly decline since October 1997, according to LSEG data.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker and a key Nvidia supplier, dropped 4.52%. Other major Taiwanese technology stocks also fell, with Foxconn losing 4.08% and Wistron declining 4.49%.

The broader Asia tech stocks sold off on Friday, following declines in U.S. peers overnight.

— Jenny Lee

Samsung Electronics names new memory chip, mobile business chiefs in leadership reshuffle

Samsung Electronics announced a leadership reshuffle Friday, naming new heads for its semiconductor and mobile businesses.

Sang Joon Hwang was promoted to president and named head of the memory business, while Sangyeun Cho was appointed president and will lead System LSI, which develops semiconductor chips including mobile processors and image sensors.

Jong Myeong Lee was promoted to president and named chief technology officer of the device solutions division, the company said.

Samsung shares fell 6% amid a wider rout in Asian tech names, following a sell-off in U.S. AI stocks.

— Jenny Lee

Alibaba shares rise 2% after robust earnings, bucking broader Asia market sell-off

Shares of Chinese tech giant Alibaba rose 2.42%, bucking a broader sell-off in Asian markets, following robust earnings.

The gains followed Alibaba's quarterly earnings report on Thursday, which showed operating income surging 443% from a year earlier to 29.12 billion yuan ($4.34 billion). Net income more than tripled to 64.42 billion yuan, helped by investment gains and improved operating performance.

Alibaba's gain stood out against a broader regional sell-off, with Japanese and South Korean technology shares sharply following overnight losses on Wall Street. Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng Index also dropped 2%.

— Jenny Lee

SoftBank shares plunge over 16% as Asian chip stocks tumble after Anthropic IPO

TOKYO, JAPAN - FEBRUARY 03: SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son delivers a speech during an event titled "Transforming Business through AI" in Tokyo, Japan, on February 03, 2025. SoftBank and OpenAI announced that they have agreed a partnership to set up a joint venture for artificial intelligence services in Japan.

Tomohiro Ohsumi | Getty Images News | Getty Images

Shares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader decline in Asian technology stocks following Anthropic's much-anticipated Wall Street debut.

SoftBank's substantial investment in Anthropic rival OpenAI has left it particularly exposed to shifts in AI investor sentiment.

Japanese chip stocks also fell sharply, with Tokyo Electron down 7.19%, Lasertec losing 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%.

The sell-off extended to South Korea, where SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics declined 6% and 4.7%, respectively.

The decline in Asian tech names follows a slide overnight in U.S. stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite dropping more than 2%.

— Jenny Lee

Thu, Nov 19 20267:50 PM EST

Japan's Nikkei plunges over 4% as inflation data raises rate hike expectations, tech stocks slide

Japan's Nikkei 225 plunged 4.5% after data released Friday showed core inflation jumping to the highest this year at 2.2%, raising expectations of another rate hike in December.

The probability of a hike next month now stands at 72%, according to LSEG data.

The index was pressured by sharp declines in tech and related names, with SoftBank Group dropping 16%, chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging over 9% , while Tokyo Electron slid 7%.

— Vinay Dwivedi

Thu, Nov 19 20267:18 PM EST

Japan's core inflation in October hits 2026 high of 2.2% as energy prices bite

Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.

Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell nearly 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.

The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $485 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL).

Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.

Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.

Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.

Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Capabilities

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

Inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.
